utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Ms. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Matthew Olmsted, Case Manager Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, for the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go into closed session now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting for the next witness can to come, can the record reflect that Muireann Dennehy is now present in the courtroom. She will be leading the next witness, and we also have our intern, Mr. Uros Zigic present as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Mr. President, we're ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to Zagreb to assist the Tribunal, Mr. Witness. Can you give us your name and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zeljko Sandor. I was born 19 March 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity, please? Did you hear me, Mr. Witness? I asked you what your ethnicity was. Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard you. Your Honour, I am Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sandor, you are about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to you that by making that declaration you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could you now read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Dennehy, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, are you able to hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, can you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sandor, do you recall giving a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal in 2000?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And turning to tab 1 of the Court's bundle could I please ask that the English version of 65 ter 2417.1 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, do you recognise the document before you to be the statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, this is the statement that I gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And looking at the first page of that document, can you please look at the signatures at the bottom of the first page and tell me whether you recognise any of those signatures.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And before testifying today, did you have an opportunity to review a translation of the statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when you reviewed the statement, I believe you had a number of corrections to make. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now if I can refer you to paragraph 29 of your statement, and at that paragraph you said ... at paragraph 29 your statement said: "Six or seven men were selected from the buses ..." Is there anything that you would like to correct in relation to that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, there is something I would like to correct here.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what that is.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Those people were not separated from our bus. They had already been separated from the other buses or from the column.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And were those men taken from the bus that you were on?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now turning to paragraph 33, your statement notes that the convoy was stopped at a cattle farm in either one of those towns, referring to the previous paragraph where you referred to Aljmas and Erdut. And you say "I can't remember which one." Is there anything you would like to correct in relation to this paragraph, that's paragraph number 33?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, there is something I would like to correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Please explain to me what you would like to correct.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: This was the cattle farm in Bogojevo and not in either Aljmas or Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sandor, if you were asked the same questions today about the material in your statement, would you give the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, my answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of this statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, my statement is accurate and truthful.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this statement as 65 ter number 2417.1 and asks that it be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a document from 2003, I believe, which is a series of corrections that were made when the witness attested to his statement which is the same one that is now being tendered before Your Honours and this Chamber. And these corrections have not been gone over with the witness and some of them are material changes, I would suggest. I don't know how important they are, but they are material changes, they run to more than a page. So I'm not sure how the Prosecution wishes to handle this. The witness has answered as he has answered, but then he did also make this attestation in 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has reviewed this document and it is of the view that these are clarifications rather than corrections to the witness's statement. The witness has reviewed this document and any clarifications that need to be made to the statement will be done so now during the witness's further testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you're not tendering that document, Ms. Dennehy?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: That is correct. The Prosecution's understanding is that we were only allowed to tender one statement and that is the underlying statement that I have referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what you're saying is that these clarifications will transpire to -- through the testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I don't think that complies with the requirements of 92 ter, but we will not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, the Bench considers that document with clarification as being part of the original statement, so you should tender it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I can certainly do so now if Your Honours will allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But it's a different 65 ter number; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: It is indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So let's admit and mark both documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement under 65 ter 02417.1 will be Exhibit P347. And if Your Honours -- if counsel for the Prosecution can provide the 65 ter number for the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: The 65 ter number is 02512.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 02512 will then become Exhibit P348.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Dennehy. I suppose that will save some time in your direct examination because you don't have to ask those questions anymore?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And why are you not currently employed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I'm retired due to disability.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what disabilities do you suffer from that caused you to retire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, you mean disabilities with regard to the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think you should say so to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, do the abilities [sic] from which you suffer and the reason for your retirement, do those relate to the events of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, at paragraph 12 of your statement you refer to negotiations that were taking place in relation to the evacuation of civilians from the Borovo factory complex. Where did these negotiations take place?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: The first round of negotiations with regard to the evacuations of civilians took place in the village of Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what were the parties that participated in those negotiations in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were members of the ZNG and the police on the one side and members of the JNA on the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what happened at those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: According to what I know, the negotiations were interrupted by Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan. He had his say in the final outcome of the negotiations. He interrupted the negotiations and he did not want to proceed negotiating with the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Simply, the negotiations fell through. Our representatives who went to Dalj to negotiate returned to Vukovar, and as far as I know, before they returned Arkan's men had beaten them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Who did Arkan's men beat?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Ivica Banusic, Marko Filkovic and three other lads that were there. Those people attended the negotiations as representatives of the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, you were injured by shrapnel at the Borovo shoe factory on the 18th of November, 1991. I would now like to show you a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Would the court officer please display 65 ter 3038 and that's at tab 3 of the witness's bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, do you recognise the map in front of you? Can I please ask you to repeat your answer, Mr. Sandor. I'm afraid I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what is this a map of?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: This is a map of the general area of Vukovar and the city of Vukovar itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please circle for me the position of the Borovo factory complex on the map in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has now indicated where the Borovo factory complex is on the map. I can indicate for you if you would like or I'm not quite sure how we proceed from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It depends on what you want to do, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I would now ask that 65 ter 3038 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The one marked by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is there a way for us to be able to see the markings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the Registrar could try to show it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It's in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's more or less Vukovar. [Microphone not activated]. I'm sorry. You tender it, no objection, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map as marked by the witness will be Exhibit P349.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, I would now like to take you forward to paragraph 33 of your statement where you describe your journey from Vukovar on the buses and where you said earlier that the convoy stopped at Bogojevo. What happened to you at Bogojevo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: JNA troops entered Bogojevo and they started pulling out detainees one by one from the bus. We were beaten up there and we were tied. They threw us down a slope by a long white building. They threw us against that wall, tied up, and they told us to go to a place called Gornje Bare, that a group would come and they will take us to Gornje Bare. And they did come later on, that group did appear later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what injuries did you suffer as a result of these beatings at Bogojevo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: A soldier of the JNA came and told me to crawl out of the bus. When I reached the front door, two other guys pulled me out of the bus and handed me over to the other two. There were four of them around me and they brutally started beating me up with all sorts of things. They kicked me. They hit me with rifle-butts. I was beaten up black and blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: At paragraph 41 you say that you were taken to a prison at Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that the court officer display 65 ter 2964. That's at tab 6 of the Court bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, do you recognise the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: What is this a map of?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: This is a map which depicts one part of Croatia and one part of Serbia and the border between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please indicate on the map the place where you were detained in Serbia in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I please ask that 65 ter 2964 be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map as marked by the witness will be Exhibit P350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, at paragraph 43 of your statement you said that when you arrived at Sremska Mitrovica, you were forced to run through a gauntlet of prison guards who beat you. What did they beat you with?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: They were beaten by rubber police batons, by fists. We were kicked. We were hit with rifle-butts, with sticks. They used all sorts of things to beat us up. Mostly police batons and some wooden sticks, like broomsticks of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can please ask that the record be amended at page 54, that's at line 2. It currently says: "They were beaten ..." Can I ask that the witness clarify who was beaten. I understand this to be interpretation point.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter misspoke. The witness said: We were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, at Sremska Mitrovica you were taken to a cell. How many men were in the cell with you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Anything between 120 and 130 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And how would you describe the cell and the conditions in the cell?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Its footprint was about 60 square metres. There were no beds. There was a wooden floor and we were like sardines in a tin. There was no room to walk around, to turn around, to go to the loo. Let me put it simply. You had to keep your original position for hours because there was no room to manoeuvre. We were compressed in that room. We could not turn around.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: What happened when the guards entered the cell?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Whenever the door was opened, whenever we heard a key being turned in the lock, we had to stand up, face the wall. We had to bow our heads and put our hands behind our back. So whenever we were about to get in contact with a guard, that's how we had to stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where did you wash?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: We had a bathroom in the basement, but we did not wash ourselves very often. For example, for the first month or so we never washed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And why did you not wash for the first month?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: They didn't allow us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, I'd now like to ask you about Damir Kiralj. How did Damir look when you saw him in the cell?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Damir Kiralj was one of the four persons who had been brought to the cell before us. He was already there when we were brought in and he was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And how did he look, given that he was seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: He was covered with blood. He was exhausted. He had open wounds on the chest and on the back. He had dark hair, he had a beard. He was visibly exhausted and he kept on asking us for water. He could still speak when we arrived in the cell. He was still half conscious and he kept on asking us to give him water to drink.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And did Damir survive?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: How were you treated by the JNA soldiers when they took you for interrogations at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Every time when I was taken for interrogation, and not just I but everybody, we were beaten up by the guards who were members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Court those beatings?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Look here, one guard would come to the door and would call my name. I would leave the cell. I would be taken to an officer to be interrogated. And on the way, one or two or more of them were there. They daunted me. They shoved me. They started kicking me ever so lightly at first and then more heavily with sticks and they shoved me to and fro. And if I were to fall down, then they would kick me and then they would start daunting me, saying, "Look at Ustasha, he's weak, he cannot stand." And if I would remain standing, then they would continue beating me on the shoulders, in the neck, on the back, all over the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where did the guards bring you for those interrogations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: They took us to JNA officers. Those who were probably one of them investigating judge, the other in charge of the prison. In any case, they were JNA officers and they were sitting in separate rooms that looked like offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when you were brought to those offices, did you enter them immediately?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Sometimes yes, sometimes no.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what would happen when you didn't enter immediately?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Sometimes I would be standing by the door for hours with my head bowed and hands behind the back. I was not allowed to move or look sideways. I was not allowed to address anybody. They did not give me water to drink. And then when I entered, sometimes the officer would say, "No, no, I didn't want to talk to this guy, I wanted to see somebody else." And then without a word of explanation, they would just take me back to my cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you used to have to stand with your head bent and your hands behind your back. What would happen if you raised your head?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: One of the guards was always there observing us. If we lifted our heads, he would come and punish us by beating us. We would suffer corporal punishment for moving slightly or for disobeying those orders that the guards had previously given us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And at paragraph 65 of your statement, you say that you had to carry out work and one of those jobs was to scrub a stair step for hours. Can you please describe that incident.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes. One day I was taken out from my cell and they took me up the stairs made of stone that a guard had spilled water on and he told me to sweep and wipe the stairs, and I did so for an hour with my own bare hands. I spent an hour rubbing the steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Were the beatings of prisoners ever recorded at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: You mean by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, if they were recorded by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: What special treatment did deserters of the JNA receive while at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Those people were rounded up and taken to isolation cells where they were mistreated every day in various ways, from beatings to singing Chetnik songs. They called these people out every day and mistreated them mentally and physically.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness also said something about a light bulb that the interpreter did not understand. Could he repeat maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, I'm afraid we didn't capture everything that you said. Could you please repeat the part where you mentioned a light bulb.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I said those people were isolated, in isolation cells, only one person per cell, and they were exposed to physical and mental torture by the guards on a daily basis, the military guards. Apart from beatings, they had to sing Chetnik songs. They had to bark like dogs at light bulbs and say things like, "Long live Serbia." And they were at the mercy of the military guards, or rather, the military policemen who guarded them every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please describe what happened to Mr. Musa.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Mr. Musa is a defector from the Yugoslav People's Army who joined the Croatian defence forces. He was in an isolation cell and he was one of the people who were mistreated in those ways I described.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: At paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, it's that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we will -- Mr. Witness, the Court will take its second break, come back at 12.45, and we will continue with your testimony at that time. Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Dennehy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, can you please explain what happened to Nikola Cibaric?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Nikola Cibaric was captured, taken to the basement of that building which was a school. He was beaten up and his genitals were cut.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: At paragraph 89 of your statement you describe how you were interrogated by Mr. Salic, a member of the KOS. What, if anything, did he make you eat during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question again, Mr. Sandor. What, if anything, did he make you eat during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: He made me eat salt and pepper.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And how much salt and pepper did he make you eat?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: A couple of tablespoons, not full but four or five tablespoons of salt and pepper. There were two dishes. I had to take some salt from one and some pepper from the other and put it in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what did you do after eating the salt and pepper?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I was choking. It was very difficult to swallow. I returned to my cell, had some water, and I threw up. I threw it all up and, of course, I had pain in my stomach, a burning feeling in my mouth. The inside of my mouth was bloody and cracked.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, can you describe for the Trial Chamber what injuries you had while at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: My lungs were damaged. It was something like a concussion of the lungs. My chest is deformed. My ribs were broken. There's damage to my spine and my hearing and vision are also damaged. I had problems with headaches and I had a concussion of the brain.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what caused all of these injuries that you describe?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: It was caused by the physical torture inflicted by the guards, by the military police at the camp, the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, what happened on the 14th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: We were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: In Nemetin, near Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And how did you feel on that day when you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: That day was the longest day in my life. It was longer than all the days I'd spent in the camp, and you can imagine that a day in the camp is an eternity.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And how has the detention at Sremska Mitrovica affected you and your family's lives?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I still have problems nowadays. While I was single I was withdrawn, I was trying to run away from myself, something was always chasing me. I still feel somehow poisoned, damaged. I am often dizzy, very depressed. Contacts with various officials are very difficult for me. I'm nervous. I shake. I sleep 10, 15 minutes a night and then don't sleep for hours. For years I didn't allow my bedroom door to be closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my questions for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Sandor. Can you see and hear me?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I can see you and I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell. I appear on behalf of Mr. Hadzic and I will be asking you a few questions. If anything is unclear, please feel free to ask for further clarification or details and I'll do my best. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were describing during your questions to the -- your answers to the questions by the Prosecutor that you came across some deserters in the prison at Sremska Mitrovica. Do I understand that they on occasion were detained along with you in the same cell or were they always separated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: They were with me in the cell for a while. That's how I know they were deserters and I know they were taken to isolation cells. And some of them were brought back from the solitary cell back to ours, so I know what they had gone through while in isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And approximately how many of these deserters did you meet?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... is one. And there was an active-duty NCO of the JNA, his name was Ivica, I don't know his last name, he was with me in the room number 8. They took him to the isolation cell and then he appeared before the court in Belgrade. He was an NCO of the JNA and he defected to the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The beginning of your answer was cut off, but would it be correct to say that you met three deserters or did you meet more than three deserters or less?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Two, two. I mentioned Musa and that active-duty sergeant of the Yugoslav People's Army. Ivica was his name and I don't remember his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did they inform you whether desertions were widespread in the JNA at the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to confirm that the previous occasions on which you have given statements, and I understand that you, of course, have given one statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in the year 2000 and then you corrected or made some amendments to that statement in 2003. And in 2004 -- excuse me, in 1994 you spoke to someone who was apparently from something called the Commission of Experts. It was a woman named Nancy Paterson. Do you remember having given that statement in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So other than the statements I've just mentioned, have you ever given any other statements to anyone about the -- about your experiences?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I gave those statements to the Croatian justice authorities, their investigation authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When did you give that statement and to whom?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I think it was in 1993 or 1994 at the Ministry of Justice of Croatia. The person was Ivica Crnkovic, and it was an occasion when ten of us former camp inmates gave statements. And I believe I also gave some statement last year to the Croatian investigating authorities regarding events in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever see your -- the content of your interview put into a note or put into a statement form which you then reviewed? Or was it, rather, that you were interviewed and then you never saw a statement or a note to review?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Which statement do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm referring to the now two interviews that you've described as having had with the Croatian authorities, one that you recall having occurred in 1993 or 1994 and the second having occurred last year.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity to see, to review, that last statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's the one from last year? Not sure if my question came through, sir. You say that you reviewed one statement, the second. And I just want to confirm, the statement that you reviewed was the statement that you say you gave during an interview last year with the Croatian authorities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter doesn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, could you just try one more time. The audio seems to be a little bit off. I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I said that's correct. I saw that statement given to the Croatian authorities last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you never saw a statement that was produced after your interview in 1993 or 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No, I don't think I saw that one -- at least I don't remember seeing it. I saw that statement that you just mentioned. Can you help me? I don't know whether it was somebody from The Hague Tribunal, but it's the one you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I was about to say the statement I gave to Ivica Crnkovic at the Ministry of Justice, that one I never saw, but it was a summary of my statement on one or two pages but I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, could you just repeat the last name of the person to whom you gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: It was the minister of justice of the Republic of Croatia, Ivica Crnkovic, C-r-n-k-o-v-i-c. I think he was the minister of justice at the time in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And have you ever been interviewed for a television documentary about events during the battle of Vukovar, in particular in Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: For a documentary, I don't think so. But I was once invited to a programme dedicated to the anniversary of the fall of Vukovar, to a radio/television show. And I gave one interview to something that is called Index, and I'm not sure whether it's a news agency or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the programme that was dedicated to the anniversary of the fall of Vukovar, do you recall what radio or television station that was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Croatian Radio Television, channel 1. It was the headlines of the news programme at noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And have you yourself seen documentaries on television about the battle of Vukovar, in particular the events in Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And your comrades in arms have been interviewed extensively as part of those documentaries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: If you allow me to say this, you probably mean the series called: "Heros of Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Some of my comrades in arms did give interviews for that series. I, myself, didn't want to be a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct you to paragraph 3 of your statement, the second-last sentence, it should be page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I just ask whether the witness has an enumerated B/C/S version of his statement there? I'm not sure whether I should be asking the Registrar there or whether I should be asking the Prosecutor here.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I believe the witness has a numbered copy, but I would like the Registrar to confirm just in case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I can confirm that the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, ought I to direct that through you or should I simply ask the Registrar whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Registrar just confirmed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the second-last sentence of paragraph 3 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What it says is, in English, and I'll read it: "At this time my Serb neighbours were being mobilised into the military. None of the Croats were being mobilised. In the beginning, there was no defensive organisation among the Croat civilians." Now, I just want to understand the first sentence there: "At this time my Serb neighbours were being mobilised into the military." Are you saying that your Serb neighbours were starting to take up arms in preparation for a civil war?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. And then you say: "None of the Croats were being mobilised. In the beginning there was no defensive organisation among the Croat civilians." So do I understand your statement to be saying that at this time, in May 1991, Serbs were arming themselves and preparing for civil war but Croats were not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: At that time not so much. Only the Croatian police were arming themselves. Civilians had no access to weapons, at least not in the area about which I testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we can just go up two sentences from the sentence that I've just been looking at, you described some men coming to look for you and you say: "I was known to be very friendly with Zadro Blago, who was one of the main leaders and organisers of the Croatian defence." What was the Croatian defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Blago Zadro was at that time a member of the Croatian police. The Croatian Democratic Union was in the process of being established, but I was no part of it. If you let me clarify, I was friends with Blago Zadro along completely different lines, nothing to do with the party or the military or the police. We were just friends. At that time, the whole of 1991 and 1992, I was not a member of any political party --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: -- my relationship with late Blago Zadro has not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me just cut you off there. I will be asking you a series of questions and you will be able to answer these questions, I assure you. But my first question, just to keep the focus is: What was the Croatian defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: That was the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Then why didn't you say "Croatian police," instead of the "Croatian defence"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I have my own viewpoint. I think this sentence is taken out of context. When I say "our men," I mean the Croatian police and the ZNG, the Home Guards Corps. You can make your own conclusions from that sentence. At that time, the Croatian police was the only armed formation, if we are talking about March, April, and May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, here we're talking -- you, not we, you are talking in your statement about May 1991. You've used this term "Croatian defence." I think I now hear you clarifying that you consider the Croatian defence to be the police and the ZNG. Is that right? Or did the Croatian -- when you use the term "Croatian defence," does it encompass anything else?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: The Croatian defence includes only the Croatian police and later the Home Guards Corps, once it was established. If you let me clarify, beginning with the events in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, the Croats had night guards organised by the Croatian Democratic Union, but they were not armed apart from those people who were licensed by the Croatian police to carry a weapon. So at that time it was only the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how many people were licensed to carry weapons by the Croatian police, according to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I could not tell you that. I've already told you that I was not a member of any political party or any other organisation at the time. When I joined the Croatian side it was spontaneously and it was after the armed operations by Serbs against Croatian police in Borovo Selo. That was already the beginning of the armed conflict. Before that, Croats were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, is it correct to say - and I believe this is -- this follows from your previous statement - you say that members of the night guards were organised by the Croatian Democratic Union and that then members of these night guards were licensed by the Croatian police to carry weapons. Is that the situation in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I think there must be a misunderstanding. In May, only the Croatian police carried weapons. Civilians at that time did not have weapons. More precisely, in early May, let's say, that was the situation, perhaps later. Civilians stood guard but not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you're saying that these night guards that were organised by the HDZ were walking around unarmed, with no weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the night guards walking around with no weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I was just going to explain. There was always a police officer with them and police officers were licensed to carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At what stage did the police start to licence other members of the night guard to carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I can speak about myself. In the month of June I joined the ZNG and I was issued with a weapon. So the answer would be as of the beginning of June onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I understand that about yourself. Do you know of others who were licensed to carry weapons who participated in these night guards? I don't want names. The question is simply: Do you know whether others were licensed to carry weapons at part of these night guards?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: There was always a police officer licensed to carry weapons who accompanied those night guards. At that time, civilians were not licensed to carry weapons. Perhaps somebody had a weapon or, for example, a rifle hidden in the house, but I wouldn't know that. At that time, civilians did not carry weapons legally. They acted as an extended arm or an extended ear or eye, as it were, for those police officers who were licensed to carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was Mr. Zadro part of the police or was he a part of the night guard? What was his function and role in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Mr. Zadro was a member of the Croatian police. He was a member of the Vinkovci police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was he a career police officer or had he joined shortly before May 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I don't know that, so I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Weren't you friends with him in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: If you listened to me carefully, we were friends before the war. In the war I saw him very seldom in passing. I did not have many occasions to talk to him once the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, before the war when you were friends with him, what occupation did he have, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: He was an employee of the Borovo factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge as to when he left that employment and became a policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 10 of your statement, you say that you wore the green camouflage uniform that the Croat army now wears. "I had been issued with a rifle and uniform by the crises council." Am I right to say that you've just testified you received your rifle in June 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you repeat the name of the month. You referred to the sixth month of the year, yes, June. June 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that also when you received your uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And those were both from the -- what you describe in your statement as the crises council?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I would like to correct that. I was issued with weapons in the office of the chief of the defence council of the city of Vukovar. At that time it was also known as the crisis council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you ever use the term "Krizni Stab" to refer to that, of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, that office for defence was reappointed as the Crisis Staff once the war started or once the war became imminent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And who was a part of that council or -- yeah, who was a part of that council? Who were the members?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: The chief of the Crisis Staff was Tomislav Mercep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was anyone else a part of the council?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: There were other people there, but I didn't know them. There was a whole structure of men belonging to the Crisis Staff, but I did not know any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When did that structure come into existence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know that I was issued with a weapon in the month of June. I don't know when they became operational. I suppose that that coincided with the democratic changes that were happening in the course of 1990 and 1991, but I'm not sure of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when you received your weapon, did you receive it from a depot in which there were other weapons? Did somebody bring it to you? How did you actually get your rifle? What were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I reported to the Crisis Staff and the person who organised defence at the time took me to the Crisis Staff. On the order of the chief of the Crisis Staff, Tomislav Mercep, I was issued with a weapon. There was a depot and a person -- the person in charge of the depot issued me with an automatic rifle and 150 rounds for it and that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So did I understand that you reported to the Crisis Staff on the order of the chief of the Crisis Staff, Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: A slight correction, sir, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I did not report to the Crisis Staff on the order of the chief of the Crisis Staff. The person who organised those night guards in Nove Banijske took me to the chief of the Crisis Staff and I was issued with a weapon on his order. Once I already reported to the Crisis Staff, it was the chief of the Crisis Staff who said that I should be issued with a weapon. That was his instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What I'm interested in knowing is whether you voluntarily went to the Crisis Staff or whether you were conscripted or ordered. Whoever may have given the order, were you conscripted or did you volunteer?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, we have a note from the Prosecution of their conversation with you, I believe it was yesterday, and you indicate that the attack on Vukovar started on the 4th of July, 1991. And you specify that that was an attack of combined artillery and infantry. Now, I'll get right to the point without beating around the bush. Isn't it true that the first combined infantry and artillery attack on Vukovar occurred -- started on the 24th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, that was a JNA attack. On the 4th of July paramilitary Serb units attacked Borovo Naselje. I'm talking about the formations that were established between March and July 1991. Those Serbs were mobilised and joined those paramilitary units. Those were Serb paramilitary units. I don't know how else to call them. Those were local Serbs who acted in concert with those who had come from Serbia. So that was not a JNA attack on Croatians; it was an attack of the local Serbs against the local Croatians, and that took place on the 4th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And artillery was not involved in that, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "artillery"? It was a mortar attack. It was a combined infantry and mortar attack. Those mortars were of smaller calibre. I don't know how else I am supposed to explain that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was a much larger-scale attack that occurred on the 21st of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When do you, as best you can recall, believe that the first major attack occurred on Vukovar -- if I could add to that, involving the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the 14th or 15th of September when JNA sent its tanks to Trpinska road and their attack ensued from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And Croat forces managed to destroy many of those tanks; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, in fact, you succeeded in repelling the attack as a whole, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you did that despite being massively outgunned and outnumbered; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you were able to disable the tanks using 64-millimetre Zolja rocket-launchers; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you also have 90-millimetre Osa rockets?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, there were Osa rockets as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that the Serb forces at this stage sent their column straight down the middle of the road and thought they could just steamroll over you; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It seems that they overestimated their own force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly that your tactic, the tactic of the Croat forces, was to line the roads on either side of where the tanks were proceeding and would shoot using infantry from one side as a decoy and would then launch rocket attacks from the other side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, but we did not launch rockets. We launched RPGs and Zoljas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And wasn't the idea that you would attempt -- given that you had a limited number of rockets, you would attempt to disable the front, the lead vehicle, and the rear vehicle of the convoys, thus pinning in the remaining vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, that was the tactic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And concealment was, for you, essential to be able to make this tactic work; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you hid in basements and in houses, behind windows and doors behind which you had -- you were fortified with sandbags; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Well, we used houses as shelters. We were not overly fortified. There were no bunkers. We used houses and ruins. Because a lot of the houses had been destroyed by tanks previously and those ruins, those remains, of the former houses were used as shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you were so successful at destroying tanks and armoured vehicles that the road on which this attack occurred, Trpinja road became known as "tank cemetery" amongst Croat forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is it right to say that generally these convoys would consist of a tank up front leading armoured personnel carriers with soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Well, one could put it that way although they were not travelling in convoys. They move forward in a combat formation rather than a convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And your aim was to immobilise the combat formation by disabling the front and the lead vehicles; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, once you would immobilise the column, were there ever occasions in which Serb soldiers tried to exit the APCs in the middle of the convoy and surrender?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I don't know that. If you will allow me, Trpinjska road is wide enough so the convoy could manoeuvre. We did not pin it down if we destroyed the tank at the front and the tank at the rear. They could still manoeuvre. They could pull themselves out. And if you're asking me whether soldiers got killed, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you did succeed in immobilising APCs as well as tanks; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And on those occasions, did it ever occur, did you ever see or did you ever hear, that Serb soldiers attempted to exit the APCs or any other armoured vehicle and tried to surrender?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I don't know that. There were cases when those lads were captured and taken to the Vukovar Hospital. I myself was not an eye-witness. I just heard stories to that effect. At that time, I never got in close contact with a live soldier. Most of the soldiers managed to return to Trpinja unscathed once they got out from those destroyed vehicles. We never used the situation in order to try and kill them when you were withdrawing. They always had an opportunity to withdraw from a vehicle. I myself never captured anybody, but I also never saw a situation when withdrawing soldiers, retreating soldiers, were shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say they always had an opportunity to withdraw. Did they ever have an opportunity to surrender?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: As I've told you, I was not in a situation to see a soldier surrendering to us. I was not in a situation where I could receive a surrendering soldier. There must have been some who surrendered. I myself was never in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, where were you stationed during the battle of Vukovar mainly, if there was one location?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: In the Crepulje sector, in the direction of Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you weren't on the front line?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you weren't on the front line, do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: It was the front line. It was the front line in the Borovo Selo sector, in Crepulje to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you ever see any prisoners, Serb prisoners, being brought back from Trpinjska road or elsewhere to the hospital or to any detention facility?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you have any idea how many Serb soldiers died in the battle of Vukovar approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I don't know. There are speculations about that number and the number of those casualties is exaggerated. Some say 15.000, some say 20.000. It doesn't seem real. It's far-fetched, much exaggerated, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And after the -- this engagement that you've described as occurring in September along the Trpinska road when many armoured JNA vehicles were immobilised, did the JNA start to change its tactics as to how it sought to invade Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How did that change?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Open frontal attacks stopped and were replaced by large-scale shellings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in order to avoid being attacked on either side of the roads, didn't they start to destroy houses on those either sides of the roads and move through the neighbourhoods? Wasn't that how they responded to the success of Croat forces against their columns?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I should have broken up my question. What is "no" answering to? What do you mean "no"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is from the point of view of a Croatian defender. If you start moving in a convoy of some ten vehicles and if you start opening fire from your starting point to provide support to the APC and your manpower, that's an open attack. That's your intention, to attack. You -- and the other side has the impression that it is being attacked. You open fire. It is not your intention to negotiate peacefully. If you set out from Trpinja and if you start opening fire, your intention was to destroy. None of our artillery assets could reach as far as Trpinja. We couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, all I'm asking is: Isn't it true that the JNA was moving through these houses because you had devastated their armour as they moved down the roads?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't understand. Are you referring to armoured vehicles or manpower?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to tanks. Instead of moving their tanks down the roads on which they were --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I've told you already. I've told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At paragraph 7 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, could you lay some foundation about "these houses." I'm a little bit lost. What is happening here? I mean on the ground. Obviously you seem to say that something different happened after the Trpinjska road incident or battle or whatever you call it, but what did happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I haven't laid the foundation I was hoping to at the beginning of page 78. Let me just go back. I thought I received a different answer than I actually did receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back and ask you, after the Trpinjska road battle in which many tanks were immobilised, is it correct that the JNA started to attempt to move along the neighbourhoods through houses on either sides of the road? Is that -- did they change their tactic along those lines?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. Tanks could not go through those houses. The foundations are very solid, very firm. A tank cannot go through a house like that. It just can't pass, so I don't understand what you're asking. A tank cannot pass through. It can destroy a house with a shell, but it cannot go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And didn't they seek to destroy these houses with shells to clear a path for the tanks? Isn't that precisely what occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you don't know --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I don't see why.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I won't take the matter further, sir. I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 7 of your statement and you say that: "The JNA were positioned between Borovo Selo and Borovo Naselje. They could supervise the Serb civilians leaving the area and the paramilitaries entering the area." Can you tell me what period you're referring to in that paragraph? Is it throughout the battle of Vukovar or starting as of what date?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: It started with the events in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May until the 4th of July, so it's those two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And your understanding was that the JNA was controlling whether or not to allow paramilitaries into the area; is that right? I'm not sure if we got the answer.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA was controlling entries of paramilitaries from Borovo Selo to Borovo Naselje and exits of paramilitaries from Borovo Selo to Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, at paragraph 19 you describe being lined up in front of the commerce building on the 19th of November. And then you describe, in the following paragraphs, being transported and eventually ending up as you've described earlier today at Bogojevo. And what I'd like to ask you is first a general question. From the time that you were lined up at the commerce building until you arrive in Bogojevo, was it your understanding that throughout that entire time you were in the custody of one or another unit of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: If you mean the active personnel of the JNA, no. As for the JNA, there was only one officer, that major I mentioned, who was an active-duty officer and the rest were all reservists and paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, by "JNA," I meant active-duty, regular JNA, or reserve.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, there was active-duty personnel, for instance, that officer, and there were people dressed in JNA uniform with the JNA insignia, including the five-point star.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the one part of your description that leaves it unclear as to who is escorting you is your description of moving from the Komerc building to where you were picked up by buses. You say that you were picked up by three buses. Now, my question for you is: Between the Komerc building and the time when you were picked up by three buses, which you describe at paragraph 27 of your statement, who was it who actually escorted you there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: We were escorted by paramilitaries. When I say "paramilitary," I mean men who had different insignia from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was this Gojkovic with them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did the major go along or did he not go along?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I don't know whether the major went the whole way but he was there when people were getting off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could tab 1 of the Defence list be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, earlier we were discussing -- the document is 03256. Now, earlier we were discussing the 4th of July and it's fair to say that this is a date that sticks out in your memory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, first of all, I should ask you to make it clear for the record and not have any confusion, this is a statement that you say was extracted from you with physical abuse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Sorry. This is ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I believe there is an error with the hardcopy document -- was contained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The document contained -- is obviously not the one related to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear what the -- I didn't hear what the Registrar said, if anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The document contained in the Defence binder is not -- that it's -- this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is not the document about this witness -- I seem to remember that we have seen exactly the same --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Definitely not the one under the title at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, you're -- there is a sound problem there because we can't -- we hear the beginning of your sentence and then the end of it, but not the substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could I add a bit of information that possibly could get around this problem? The document as well as being on our list was also at -- was also at tab 7 of the Prosecution's original list. And I don't know whether the Registrar took the original list or took the revised list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I seem to remember that we have seen exactly the same document but about another witness. Perhaps the confusion is there. I even think that it is -- that it has the same date on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When I look at the front page of the document, I do see the witness's name indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The one on the screen , indeed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I believe the number is correct. So I'm not actually sure what the difficulty is, because unfortunately I can't hear the Registrar in the location of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you -- can you use the witness's microphone? Because yours is obviously not working well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Sure, Your Honour. The document that is contained, the hard copy document in the Defence binder isn't the one that was called by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood. The document --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The table of contents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] -- of the documents to be used with this witness that was provided by Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] -- lists one document that was called by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Under 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] With 65 ter number 3256; however, document with 65 ter number 3256 is not the one --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I don't know whether you have the Prosecution's bundle --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Not contained in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- but if you could look and see --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- whether you have the old bundle, you will see tab 7 of the old bundle would be the document that I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that is the Prosecution's old bundle, Mr. Registrar, tab 7. Would that be the document with the witness's name on it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I don't think so because the document under tab number 7 in the Prosecution binder is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We have a problem here, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, if I may, and with the optimistic, perhaps, expectation that perhaps there would be no objection, I would propose to read the section of the document that I wish to use and elicit the remark or any response from the witness because that's what's significant here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Registrar tells me that we could try to broadcast the document we have on the screen to the screen in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether that works. And in the meantime, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: If I may assist, Your Honours, this document was shown to the witness and the witness may have a copy with him still or the investigator may have a copy of that document. So it might be helpful to ask whether the witness is in possession of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But before we can ask the witness whether he has a document, we should be able to show it to him because if not -- so let's see what the broadcast solution would bring. In the meantime, Mr. Gosnell, I see the time. How long do you think you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I can wrap this up very shortly. I would say within five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. They have it on the screen now. And then re-direct, Ms. Dennehy, just to know where we go?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I will only have one or two questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So the document is on the screen in Zagreb, Mr. Gosnell, so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Sandor, I'm sorry, I understand that you've seen this document in preparation for your testimony. And just to make it clear, is it correct that this is the statement that you say was extracted from you under conditions that were oppressive by the JNA officer investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: With your leave, that's just a part of that detailed, long statement that was dictated to us. But I agree, that's the part of that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 2, please -- correction, that should be page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, sir, if you look at the -- midway down the page, the long paragraph, this statement says: "On 4 July 1991, sometime between 0900 and 1000 hours, an exchange of rifle fire was heard," and this is referring to Borovo Naselje. And the statement goes on: "I was at my uncle's, and at first we did not know what was happening ..." First of all, is it true that you were at your uncle's on this day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is it true that there was an exchange of fire at between 0900 and 1000 hours?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Statement goes on: "Sometime later we were all called to come in front of the 'Nikola Demonja,' MZ local commune and I went there together with all the others. After arriving at this commune, at some point the guard also came towards this MZ and then immediately left." Now, first of all, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And by "guard," are you referring to the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that's what actually happened; correct? That's true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The same time goes on: "This is when I heard that Serbs would be cleared out from a part of Borovo Naselje." Did you hear that at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: That was coerced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So just that sentence was the part that was inserted by the JNA investigating judge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: In this entire part, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. Was the next sentence also inserted by the JNA investigating judge or is that true? I'm not sure if my question came through. The question was: Was the next sentence also inserted by the investigating judge or was that true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Which next sentence? I did not hear that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The next sentence reads: "After a while in front of the local commune, Zoran Gotal, at least I think it was him, told us that Zadro Blago reported that Stara Banijska Street had been taken and that we could return."

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And by "return," does that mean that you had formerly lived on that street?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, before that, what does --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- the "yes, that's correct" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
