utterances.text: Does that mean that it was coerced or does it mean that -- that's not clear in the transcript, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, your second-last answer was not perfectly clear, so let me put the question to you again, hopefully more clearly. Did -- was it the investigating judge who inserted the sentence about Zoran Gotal, telling you that "Zadro Blago reported that Stara Banijska Street had been taken and that we could return." Was that true to your knowledge or was that something that had been inserted against your wish into the statement by the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: That is my statement to the effect that we were told, informed, that we could go back to Stara Banijska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And your statement goes on and you say: "We brought the guard to Nove Banijske Street where they set up a check-point. I did not have a weapon at that time ..." Now, earlier today you testified you received your rifle in June?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, and it is correct that on that day I did not have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you did --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: On that day I did not manage to get hold of my weapon. It remained in my uncle's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If there were shots being fired, why would you leave your rifle behind?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Because what we heard were not only infantry shots, but also mortar fires. I can give you an explanation about the two streets, Stara and Nove Banijske to shed some light on the events, maybe you will understand better.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let me proceed to the next sentence. "After this clearing out, it happened that literally all of the Serbs or a majority of the Serbs fled Stara Banijska and other streets." Is that part of your statement also true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No. The investigating judge inserted that and this is exactly what I was going to explain to the gentleman from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Look, there are two streets. One is Nove Banijske and Stara Banijska, two streets sharing partially the same name. Nove Banijske was held by the Croatian forces, whereas Stara Banijska was held by the Serb forces. The JNA enabled Serb civilians from Stara Banijska to be evacuated to Borovo Selo. If we are talking about that buffer zone. And then Serb paramilitaries from Stara Banijska launched attacks on Croatian check-points on Nove Banijske. They launched mortar shells and an infantry attack ensued. In other words, there were no civilians there. This was not a mopping-up operation. It was an operation to liberate Stara Banijska, where well-armed and well-organised military formations were stationed. There were no civilians because the civilians had already left and went to Borovo Selo. Perhaps you will remember that I said that I used to live in Stara Banijska; my house was there. I did not mop-up Stara Banijska. I went there to free my home. This was not ethnic cleansing. All the civilians who were on that side had already fled to Borovo Selo for their own safety because they knew that the Serbs were going to attack the Croats. All the other Serbs that remained in the area, they went completely unscathed. Not a single Serb was even slapped. They still live in Vukovar. They shared the destiny of us Croats. They live in the city of Vukovar. And those people who claimed that were killed by us during those operations are still living happily in Vukovar. I hope that the gentleman from the Defence now understands the distinction between Nove and Stara Banijska. I repeat that there were well-armed and well-organised Serb paramilitary formations who used JNA weaponry and the TO depots to attack Croats in the city of Vukovar, and they chose the 4th of July because it was formerly celebrated as the day of veterans. And that was the first open conflict between the Croats and the Serbs in the area, if we exclude hostilities by the JNA that happened previously. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, thank you very much for your answers and your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Re-direct, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, at paragraph 85 and 86, you refer to a handwritten statement that was dictated to you. When you wrote that statement, did you feel free to write what you wanted to in the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And did you agree with the entire contents of the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: At the end I had to state, I had to put down, that I gave my statement under no coercion, that it was not given under duress.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And was it true that the statement was not given under duress?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: That statement was given under duress. It was dictated to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And at paragraph 96, you refer to the proceedings before the investigative judge. Did you feel free at the time to speak openly and freely before that judge?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Sandor, I have a very short question for you and it consists of three different parts. I would like to come back to your detention in Sremska Mitrovica, in the prison there. Correct me if I'm wrong, that prison was actually established in a building -- in a school building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: No, it was an old Austro-Hungarian prison. It was a purpose-built prison. There were also classrooms for those who wanted to study. There were classrooms within the prison complex, but it was a proper prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it was a prison but there were classrooms, right? Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the basement or on the ground floor of that prison - I'm reading on page 59, lines 6 and 7 of today's transcript - you remembered that there was a man called Nikola Cibaric who was taken to the basement of that building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I apologise. You did not understand. Cibaric was not taken to Sremska Mitrovica, to the prison building there, but to Luzac which is a suburb on Vukovar. That's where he was detained in a school in the basement. It was either a school or the local commune building but it was outside of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this clarification. And my last question, you told us that there was ill-treatment, that he was ill-treated. Do you know that -- whether he survived or whether he succumbed to the wounds?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: Yes, he himself told me what he had gone through because we shared the same cell in Sremska Mitrovica subsequently. That happened to him when he was taken prisoner in Vukovar and then our paths crossed in Sremska Mitrovica when we were detained there together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your answers. Now I see where my confusion may have arisen from. He was first taken prisoner and then you were detained together later.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SANDOR
utterances.text: I apologise, I was brought to Mitrovica before him. I was the one who was in that cell first in Sremska Mitrovica, and he rejoined me later. I believe that he was brought in perhaps two or three days later. I don't know where he was in the meantime. What happened to him happened in Vukovar in the suburb called Cibac, and later on in the camps known as Begejci and Stajicevo. I don't know what they're called. He joined me in my cell later. I was there before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for all these clarifications. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sandor, this brings your testimony to an end. Thank you for coming to Zagreb to assist the Tribunal. You're now released as a witness and we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you for your patience. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.
